claimBoundary: This is one provenance-bound Codex pass. It is single-model evidence, not human, instructor, independent, classroom, or multi-judge validation.

claims: A variable is a name that refers to a stored value; the assignment operator = binds the name on the left to the value produced on the right (for objects it binds the reference, so no copy is made).
A statement sets a variable to a value using the assignment operator (=), with the name on the left and the value on the right.
Assignment is not mathematical equality — = copies a value into a variable rather than asserting two sides are equal.
A variable name may contain letters, digits, and underscores and be any length, but cannot start with a digit.
Variable names are case-sensitive, so total and Total are two different variables.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §1.3 Variables

artifact.df: A label referring to a piece of data in memory, such as 'count' in a loop.
artifact.eg: In a program, 'user_age' is the name referring to the stored integer value of 30.
artifact.mi: Thinking the name itself is the value stored, rather than a reference to it.
artifact.cx: The name is a reference to the stored value, and the assignment operator binds the name to the value produced on the right.

artifact.df: A statement that gives a name a value by putting the name on the left of = and the value on the right.
artifact.eg: x = 5 stores 5 in x in a short tracing exercise.
artifact.mi: It means the same thing as mathematical equality.
artifact.cx: In Python, = is used to set a variable, not to test whether two expressions are equal.

claims: A class defines a type of object with attributes (data) and methods (behavior); it is a blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance.
A class is a blueprint for creating objects.
Individual objects created from a class are called instances.
Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §11.1 Object-oriented programming basics; §11.2 Classes and instances

artifact.df: Individual objects created from a class are called instances.
artifact.mi: An instance is the general template for all objects.
artifact.cx: An instance is an individual object built from a class.

artifact.df: An individual object built from a class and belonging to that class's type.
artifact.eg: One specific `Rocket` object created from the `Rocket` class is an instance.
artifact.mi: An instance is the class itself.
artifact.cx: The source distinguishes the blueprint from the object made from it; the misconception collapses those into one thing and misses that instances are created from classes.

claims: Silicate minerals, built from the silicon-oxygen tetrahedron, are the most abundant rock-forming minerals; the way tetrahedra link together defines the major silicate structures.
The silicon-oxygen tetrahedron (SiO4) is one silicon atom at the center bonded to four oxygen atoms at the corners.
Tetrahedra link by sharing corner oxygen atoms into chains, sheets, or three-dimensional frameworks.
How much oxygen is shared between tetrahedra controls the silicate group — isolated tetrahedra, single chains, sheets, or frameworks like quartz.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §3.1 Silicate minerals

artifact.q: Two minerals contain the same SiO4 tetrahedra, but one forms chains and the other forms a framework. Which claim best explains the difference?
op: The amount of oxygen shared between tetrahedra controls whether they stay isolated or link into
Each tetrahedron has one silicon atom at the center bonded to four oxygen atoms at the corners
Silicate minerals are the most abundant rock-forming minerals in Earth’s crust
Tetrahedra join only by sharing silicon atoms, so structure does not vary much
artifact.ex: Correct: the degree of shared oxygen determines whether tetrahedra remain isolated or link into chains, sheets, or frameworks. The closest misconception is that the tetrahedra’s shape alone fixes the structure, but the source says the linkage pattern is controlled by how much oxygen is shared.
How much oxygen is shared between tetrahedra controls the silicate group — isolated tetrahedra, single chains, sheets, or frameworks like quartz. Single chains do not control the silicate group.

claims: Earth is layered into a thin outer crust, a thick rocky mantle, and a metallic core; the upper mantle's asthenosphere is solid rock that flows slowly by convection.
The mantle sits below the crust and above the core.
The core has both liquid and solid layers and is made mostly of iron and nickel.
The asthenosphere is mechanically weak and flows by convection currents driven by the core's heat.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §2.1 Earth's interior

artifact.df: The thick rocky layer that sits beneath the crust and above the core.
artifact.eg: The mantle is the layer identified when comparing rock structure below the crust.
artifact.mi: It is the same as the core because both are deep Earth layers.
artifact.cx: The mantle is distinct from the core; the source places it between the crust and the core.

artifact.df: The mechanically weak, flowing layer within the upper mantle.
artifact.eg: The slow movement of the upper mantle driven by convection currents.
artifact.mi: The asthenosphere is a rigid, unmoving layer.
artifact.cx: The asthenosphere is mechanically weak and flows by convection currents driven by the core's heat.

claims: The rock cycle describes how Earth's three rock families — igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic — form and continually transform into one another through geologic processes.
The rock cycle describes the major Earth materials, the processes that form them, and how they relate to each other.
Igneous rock forms when liquid rock freezes solid; lithified sediment becomes sedimentary rock; pre-existing rock can transform into metamorphic rock.
If conditions melt the rocks into magma, the cycle begins anew with new igneous rocks.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §4 The rock cycle

artifact.q: A student heats a buried sedimentary rock until minerals recrystallize without melting. Which rock family best fits the product?
artifact.ex: The best choice is metamorphic rock because pre-existing rock can transform into metamorphic rock. A common misconception is to call any altered rock igneous, but igneous rock requires liquid rock to freeze solid; here, the rock changed without melting.

artifact.q: When liquid rock cools and solidifies, what type of rock is produced according to the cycle?
artifact.ex: Option C is correct because igneous rock forms when liquid rock freezes solid. Option A is incorrect as metamorphic rock forms from pre-existing rock under different conditions, and Option B is incorrect as sedimentary rock forms from lithified sediment.

claims: Rhythm (from Greek ῥυθμός, rhythmos, "any regular recurring motion, symmetry") generally means a "movement marked by the regulated succession of strong and weak elements, or of opposite or different conditions".
"Meter may be defined as a regular, recurring pattern of strong and weak beats.
Triple metre is a metre in which each bar is divided into three beats, or a multiple thereof.

artifact.q: A score is organized so each bar is divided into three beats. Which analysis term is directly supported by that fact?
artifact.ex: Triple metre is directly supported because the defining feature is a bar divided into three beats, or a multiple thereof. The plausible misconception is to stop at meter, since meter also involves regular strong and weak beats, but that is less specific than the three-beat bar division stated here.

artifact.q: Which element describes a regular, recurring pattern of strong and weak beats?
artifact.ex: Meter is a regular, recurring pattern of strong and weak beats. Rhythm is a movement marked by the regulated succession of strong and weak elements. Meter is the pattern of beats; rhythm is the motion itself.

claims: In music, harmony is the concept of combining different sounds in order to create new, distinct musical ideas.
In these genres, chord progressions are the defining feature on which melody and rhythm are built.
Chord progressions are the foundation of harmony in Western musical tradition from the common practice era of classical music to the 21st century.
A first chord forms a 'progression' with a second chord, and a second with a third.
For example, the relative minor of C major is A minor, and in the key of A minor, the i, iv and v chords are A minor, D minor and E minor.
In many styles of popular and traditional music, chord progressions are expressed using the name and "quality" of the chords.

artifact.q: In Western musical tradition, what serves as the basis for harmony?
op: B. The combination of different sounds to create new ideas.
C. The formal evidence of the piece.
artifact.ex: Option B is correct because harmony is the concept of combining different sounds in order to create new, distinct musical ideas (Claim 0). Option A is a misconception because harmony is the concept of combining sounds, not just the melody.

artifact.q: Which statement best fits the concept of harmony in music?
op: Combining different sounds to create a distinct musical idea.
Arranging silence to replace a musical idea.
Making a melody follow a fixed drum pattern.
Choosing a key signature for a score.
artifact.ex: Combining different sounds is the correct idea of harmony; the most plausible misconception is to treat harmony as any single notational choice or a rhythm-only process.

claims: A task flow analysis diagrams the steps and decision points through which a user interacts with a system to reach a defined goal.
Task flow analysis can validate the team's understanding of user goals, common scenarios, and tasks.
A task flow should show how a user progresses through tasks to accomplish a goal.
Task flow analysis should surface obstacles that stand between users and their goals.
The diagram may include multiple possible paths, task sequences, and decision points.

artifact.q: Which method is best for showing how a user progresses through tasks to accomplish a goal?
artifact.ex: Task flow analysis diagrams the steps and decision points through which a user interacts with a system to reach a defined goal. It shows how a user progresses through tasks to accomplish a goal.

artifact.q: What can a task flow analysis help a team check?
op: Whether the team understands user goals, common scenarios, and tasks
Whether the interface uses the most modern visual trend
Whether a single observed click reveals the user's motive
Whether the product's pricing matches competitor prices
artifact.ex: It can validate the team's grasp of goals, scenarios, and tasks. One click does not prove motive, and the other options are unrelated.

claims: A task flow analysis diagrams the steps and decision points through which a user interacts with a system to reach a defined goal.
Task flow analysis can validate the team's understanding of user goals, common scenarios, and tasks.
A task flow should show how a user progresses through tasks to accomplish a goal.
Task flow analysis should surface obstacles that stand between users and their goals.
The diagram may include multiple possible paths, task sequences, and decision points.

artifact.df: A place where the flow branches based on a user choice or condition.
artifact.eg: In a payment flow, choosing between saved card and new card is a decision point.
artifact.mi: It is just a screen title or label.
artifact.cx: A decision point is a branching moment in the path, not mere page naming.

artifact.df: A diagram illustrating the sequence of steps and choices a user makes to achieve a specific objective.
artifact.eg: Mapping the steps from logging in to completing a purchase.
artifact.mi: Thinking the map must show every possible outcome, even impossible ones.
artifact.cx: The diagram must show how a user progresses through tasks to accomplish a goal.

claims: Journey mapping represents an end-to-end experience from the user's perspective so a team can see connected steps, boundaries, breakdowns, and opportunities.
A journey map should start from research about the steps users actually take and the transactions involved.
An experience map should make struggle points and candidate improvement areas visible.
A map can reveal dead ends where the user cannot continue toward the larger goal.
Journey analysis should include gaps between online and offline parts of a service.

artifact.df: A tool used to highlight areas needing improvement.
artifact.eg: Identifying where users struggle during a multi-stage service interaction.
artifact.mi: Thinking this is the same as a general research document.
artifact.cx: It makes struggle points and candidate improvement areas visible.

artifact.df: A point in the mapped experience where the user cannot continue toward the larger goal.
artifact.eg: A checkout flow that leaves no clear way to finish the purchase or recover from an error.
artifact.mi: It means the user disliked the interface or intended to leave.
artifact.cx: The claim supports a blocked path in the journey, not an inferred motive, feeling, or cause from one behavior.
